Unlike classification or regression models, which typically process fixed-size inputs and produce fixed-size outputs in a single forward pass, LLMs are autoregressive. They generate text token-by-token, where each new token depends on the entire sequence of previously generated tokens. This sequential dependency creates a fundamental tension between latency (the time it takes to generate the first token and subsequent tokens) and throughput (the number of tokens or requests processed per second).

To resolve this tension, modern LLM inference servers have evolved a sophisticated stack of optimizations. In a standard Transformer decoder, the self-attention mechanism computes attention scores between every token in the sequence and every other token. For a sequence of length $N$, the computational complexity of the attention layer is $O(N^2)$. # High-Performance LLM Inference: A Technical Deep Dive into Continuous Batching, KV Caches, and Advanced Decoding Strategies

The deployment of Large Language Models (LLMs) in production environments presents a unique set of engineering challenges that differ significantly from traditional machine learning inference. Unlike classification models that process fixed-size inputs and produce fixed-size outputs, LLMs are autoregressive generative models. They generate text token-by-token, meaning the output length is dynamic and unknown at the start of the request. This fundamental characteristic creates a complex interplay between memory bandwidth, compute utilization, and latency requirements. To serve these models efficiently, modern inference servers have evolved beyond simple static batching to incorporate sophisticated mechanisms such as continuous batching, Key-Value (KV) caching, prefix reuse, and speculative decoding. This tutorial provides a detailed technical analysis of these mechanisms, explaining how they interact to optimize the latency-throughput trade-off in high-demand LLM serving systems.

## 1. The Fundamental Bottleneck: Memory Bandwidth vs. Compute

To understand why specific optimizations are necessary, one must first understand the computational profile of LLM inference. An LLM inference step consists of two distinct phases: the **Prefill** phase and the **Decode** phase.

### The Prefill Phase
During the prefill phase, the model processes the entire input prompt in parallel. If a user submits a prompt with 1,000 tokens, the model performs matrix multiplications across all 1,000 tokens simultaneously. This phase is **compute-bound**. The GPU’s Tensor Cores are heavily utilized because the arithmetic intensity (the ratio of floating-point operations to memory accesses) is high. The model reads the weights once and applies them to a large batch of input vectors.

### The Decode Phase
During the decode phase, the model generates one token at a time. For each new token, the model must read the entire model weights from High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) to the on-chip SRAM, perform a matrix-vector multiplication (since the batch size for the new token is effectively 1 per sequence), and then write the result back. This phase is **memory-bandwidth-bound**. The GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to move from HBM to the compute units.
